subChunks.title: Mathematics for Scientists

storyBeats.txt: Mathematics is not a subject you study before science, Theodora said. It is the language science thinks in. When physicists disagreed about the orbit of Uranus, they did not discuss it — they calculated it. The calculation led directly to Neptune.

The mathematical tools scientists use most are not the exotic ones. They are proportionality, logarithms, graphs, and error analysis. Master these and you can read scientific papers. Miss them and even the most elegant experiment is opaque.

A number without units is not a scientific measurement. A graph without axes labels is not evidence. A result without an uncertainty estimate is not complete. These disciplines are not bureaucratic — they are what make measurements mean something.

subChunks.hookHtml: Every branch of science depends on mathematics — not just for calculation, but for expressing relationships between variables, communicating precision, and distinguishing signal from noise. The mathematical toolkit a scientist uses daily is not university-level calculus: it is proportional reasoning, logarithms, graph interpretation, dimensional analysis, and uncertainty. These skills underpin everything from interpreting a clinical trial to reading a physics paper.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Scientific Notation and Orders of Magnitude

Science deals with enormously large and small numbers: the diameter of a hydrogen atom is 0.0000000001 m; the mass of the Sun is 2,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg. Scientific notation expresses these as a coefficient × 10ⁿ:

  • 0.0000000001 m = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
  • 2 × 10³⁰ kg (mass of the Sun)

An order of magnitude is a factor of 10. The Sun is roughly 10³⁰ kg; a human is ~10² kg — a difference of ~28 orders of magnitude. Order-of-magnitude reasoning allows quick estimates and sanity checks.

Significant Figures

Every measurement has limited precision. Significant figures convey how precisely a quantity is known:

  • 3.14 has 3 significant figures; 3.14159 has 6.
  • 100 is ambiguous (1, 2, or 3 sig figs?); 1.00 × 10² clearly has 3 sig figs.
  • When multiplying or dividing: result has as many sig figs as the least precise input.
  • When adding or subtracting: result is rounded to the same decimal place as the least precise input.

Dimensional Analysis (Unit Tracking)

Units are not decoration — they carry physical meaning. Dimensional analysis involves tracking units through every calculation to ensure the result has the correct units.

Example: Convert 60 miles/hour to metres/second:

60 miles/hour × 1609 m/mile × 1 hour/3600 s = 26.8 m/s

Units cancel at each step. If the final units are wrong, the calculation is wrong. This technique also allows checking formulas: if the units on both sides of an equation don't match, the equation is invalid.

Proportional Reasoning and Scaling

Many scientific relationships are directly proportional (y ∝ x) or inversely proportional (y ∝ 1/x) or follow a power law (y ∝ xⁿ). Understanding proportionality allows prediction without knowing the exact constant:

  • Newton's 2nd Law: F = ma. If mass doubles and force stays constant, acceleration halves (inverse proportionality).
  • Gravitational force: F ∝ 1/r². Double the distance → force drops to 1/4.

Logarithms in Science

When quantities vary over many orders of magnitude, logarithmic scales compress the range into something comprehensible. Key scientific logarithmic scales:

  • pH scale: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. A pH of 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4 (not just 1 unit more).
  • Decibel scale: Sound intensity in dB = 10 × log₁₀(I/I₀). Every 10 dB = 10× the intensity.
  • Richter / Moment Magnitude scale: Each unit increase = roughly 32× more energy released in an earthquake.
  • Stellar magnitude: Brightness of stars.

The natural logarithm (ln, base e ≈ 2.718) appears in exponential growth and decay: radioactive decay, population growth, drug clearance from the body all follow N = N₀ × e^(kt). The half-life t₁/₂ = ln(2)/k.

Graph Interpretation

Scientists display data in graphs to reveal patterns invisible in tables. Key graph types and what they show:

  • Scatter plot: Individual data points — reveals correlation and outliers.
  • Line graph: Connects time-series or continuous data — shows trends.
  • Bar chart: Compares discrete categories.
  • Histogram: Shows frequency distribution of a continuous variable.
  • Log-log plot: If data forms a straight line on log-log axes, the relationship is a power law (y = axⁿ); the slope gives n.
  • Semi-log plot: Straight line on semi-log axes (log y, linear x) indicates exponential relationship (y = ae^(bx)).

Always examine: what are the axes labels and units? What is the scale (linear or log)? Is the y-axis zero-truncated? A graph that doesn't start at zero can make small differences look dramatic.

Uncertainty and Error Analysis

Every measurement has uncertainty. Scientists distinguish:

  • Accuracy: How close to the true value. Affected by systematic errors (calibration, bias).
  • Precision: How reproducible the measurement is. Affected by random errors.
  • Absolute uncertainty: e.g., 5.2 ± 0.3 cm — the ±0.3 is the uncertainty.
  • Relative (percentage) uncertainty: 0.3/5.2 × 100% = 5.8%

When combining measurements: for addition/subtraction, add absolute uncertainties; for multiplication/division, add relative (percentage) uncertainties. A result is only as reliable as its least precise component.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why scientists write numbers as "5.3 ± 0.2 × 10⁴" instead of just "53,000" — and what you can and cannot conclude from each form.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A chemist measures the concentration of a solution as 2.40 × 10⁻³ mol/L. (1) How many significant figures does this value have? (2) The chemist uses this concentration in the equation: Rate = k × [concentration]², where k = 3.5 × 10⁴ L/mol·s. Calculate the rate, giving the answer in correct scientific notation with the appropriate number of significant figures. (3) The measurement has an uncertainty of ±0.05 × 10⁻³ mol/L. What is the percentage uncertainty in the concentration? (4) If a reaction produces a gas with a volume of 2.4 L measured at 25°C and 1 atm, what does dimensional analysis tell you about the units of the molar volume of an ideal gas?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) 2.40 × 10⁻³ has three significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal point is significant).

(2) Rate = 3.5 × 10⁴ × (2.40 × 10⁻³)² = 3.5 × 10⁴ × 5.76 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.016 × 10⁻¹ = 0.2016. Units: (L/mol·s) × (mol/L)² = (L/mol·s) × mol²/L² = mol/(L·s). Rate = 2.0 × 10⁻¹ mol/(L·s) — rounded to 2 sig figs because k has only 2 sig figs.

(3) Percentage uncertainty = (0.05 × 10⁻³) / (2.40 × 10⁻³) × 100% = 0.05/2.40 × 100% = 2.1%.

(4) Molar volume = Volume / Amount of substance = L / mol = L·mol⁻¹. At STP (0°C, 1 atm), this is 22.4 L/mol; at 25°C and 1 atm it is 24.5 L/mol. Dimensional analysis confirms that the ratio of volume (in L) to moles gives L/mol — the correct units for molar volume.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The Richter scale measures earthquake magnitude logarithmically: each unit increase corresponds to a 10× increase in wave amplitude and roughly 32× more energy released. (1) An earthquake of magnitude 6.0 releases approximately how many times more energy than one of magnitude 4.0? (2) If the pH of unpolluted rainwater is 5.6 and acid rain is measured at pH 4.2, how many times more acidic (higher H⁺ concentration) is the acid rain? Show your working using logarithms. (3) Explain why scientists prefer to display bacterial growth curves on a semi-log graph (log population vs time) rather than a linear graph of population vs time — what does the shape of each tell you?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Two magnitude units = 32 × 32 = 1,024× more energy. An M6.0 earthquake releases approximately 1,000 times more energy than an M4.0 earthquake. (More precisely: 32² = 1,024, often rounded to 10³.)

(2) pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so [H⁺] = 10^(−pH). For pH 5.6: [H⁺] = 10^(−5.6) = 2.51 × 10⁻⁶ mol/L. For pH 4.2: [H⁺] = 10^(−4.2) = 6.31 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. Ratio = 6.31 × 10⁻⁵ / 2.51 × 10⁻⁶ = 25.1×. The acid rain is approximately 25 times more acidic (has 25× higher H⁺ concentration). Alternatively: difference in pH = 5.6 − 4.2 = 1.4; 10^1.4 = 25.1.

(3) Bacterial populations grow exponentially: N = N₀ × e^(kt), or equivalently log(N) = log(N₀) + (k/ln(10)) × t. On a linear graph, exponential growth appears as a sharply accelerating curve — it's hard to see exactly when growth began or how fast it is growing. On a semi-log graph (log population on the y-axis, linear time on the x-axis), exponential growth appears as a straight line, because log(N) is a linear function of time. The slope of this straight line directly gives the growth rate constant k/ln(10). This makes it easy to: identify the exponential phase (straight line on semi-log = truly exponential growth); compare growth rates across different conditions (steeper slope = faster growth); and identify deviations from exponential growth (lag phase at start; plateau at stationary phase). The log scale also compresses the enormous range of cell numbers (from 10 to 10¹⁰) into a manageable display.
learningObjectives: Express measurements in scientific notation with appropriate significant figures and use dimensional analysis to verify unit consistency.
Apply logarithmic reasoning to interpret pH, decibel, and Richter scale values — explaining what a one-unit change represents.
Interpret scatter plots, line graphs, and semi-log/log-log graphs to identify linear, exponential, and power-law relationships.
Calculate absolute and percentage uncertainty and apply the correct propagation rule when combining measurements.
commonMistakes: Treating significant figures as merely about decimal places — sig figs communicate measurement precision; 100 and 1.00 × 10² have very different implied precision.
Adding percentage uncertainties when adding (not multiplying) measurements — when adding/subtracting, add absolute uncertainties, not percentage uncertainties.
Assuming a straight line on a regular graph means a linear relationship — check whether the axes are log scale; a straight line on a semi-log plot indicates exponential, not linear.
Ignoring units in calculations — dimensional analysis is not optional; it catches errors that arithmetic alone cannot.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly applies significant figures rules in multiplication/division and addition/subtraction scenarios.
Accurately performs logarithmic calculations for pH, decibel, or Richter scale and interprets the result correctly.
Correctly identifies the type of relationship (linear, exponential, power law) from a described or drawn graph.
Calculates percentage uncertainty and correctly propagates it through a multiplication or division calculation.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A method of checking or deriving equations by tracking the units of each quantity — if units on both sides of an equation don't match, the equation is wrong; invaluable for unit conversion and formula verification.

Powers of ten used to compare quantities of very different sizes — the Sun is ~10²⁸ times more massive than a proton; estimating in orders of magnitude is a key scientific reasoning skill (Fermi estimation).
The formal rules for calculating how uncertainties in input measurements combine to give uncertainty in a calculated result — essential for experimental science and engineering.
A graph with one logarithmic axis and one linear axis; exponential relationships (y = ae^bx) appear as straight lines, making the growth or decay rate directly readable from the slope.

Named for physicist Enrico Fermi, the technique of making rapid order-of-magnitude estimates using reasonable assumptions — e.g., estimating the number of piano tuners in Chicago — used to check whether detailed calculations are plausible.

questions.questionHtml: When multiplying two measurements — 3.42 cm × 5.1 cm — how many significant figures should the result have?
options: 4, because 3.42 has 3 and 5.1 has 2, and you add them together
2, because when multiplying, the result has as many significant figures as the least precise input (5.1 has 2 sig figs)
3, because 3.42 has 3 significant figures and that is more than 5.1
5, because 3.42 × 5.1 = 17.442 and you keep all digits
questions.correctAnswer: 2, because when multiplying, the result has as many significant figures as the least precise input (5.1 has 2 sig figs)
questions.explanationHtml: For multiplication and division, the result should have the same number of significant figures as the input with the fewest. 3.42 has 3 sig figs; 5.1 has 2 sig figs. Therefore 3.42 × 5.1 = 17.442, which rounds to 17 (2 sig figs). The answer is 17 cm².

questions.questionHtml: A solution has a pH of 3. Another solution has a pH of 6. How many times more concentrated in H⁺ ions is the first solution compared to the second?
options: 1,000 times (10³, because pH is a logarithmic scale and a difference of 3 pH units = 10³ difference in [H⁺])
questions.correctAnswer: 1,000 times (10³, because pH is a logarithmic scale and a difference of 3 pH units = 10³ difference in [H⁺])
questions.explanationHtml: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so [H⁺] = 10^(−pH). pH 3: [H⁺] = 10⁻³; pH 6: [H⁺] = 10⁻⁶. Ratio = 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 10³ = 1,000. A common error is to subtract pH values linearly (3 − 6 = 3 times more acidic) — this ignores the logarithmic nature of the scale.

questions.questionHtml: A scientist plots bacterial population (y-axis) against time (x-axis) on a semi-log graph (log scale on y-axis) and obtains a straight line during the exponential growth phase. What does the slope of this straight line represent?
options: The total number of bacteria at any given time
The doubling time of the bacterial population
The growth rate constant — a steeper slope means faster exponential growth
The carrying capacity of the environment
questions.correctAnswer: The growth rate constant — a steeper slope means faster exponential growth
questions.explanationHtml: On a semi-log plot, exponential growth N = N₀e^(kt) becomes log(N) = log(N₀) + (k/ln10) × t — a straight line with slope k/ln10. A steeper slope means a larger k (faster growth rate). The doubling time can be derived from k (t₁/₂ = ln2/k), but the slope itself is the growth rate constant, not directly the doubling time or total numbers.
